title: Signature Walker
body:
The Signature Walker is the Signature edition's human baseline: the same 1.4 meters per second as ordinary walking, described as the pace of a Signature traveler on foot, covering five kilometers in an hour on level ground.

Reference speed: 1.4 m/s. Time to cover 100 km at this speed: 19.84 hours; time to cover the Earth-Moon distance at this speed: 8700.64 years; time to cover one astronomical unit: 3386098.53 years.

Its limit is the same body as the public reference: hills, loads, and fatigue. The Signature edition changes the framing and the name, never the physics, and it says so. Standard math: c = 299,792,458 m/s is the absolute limit; this reference is far below c, so time dilation is negligible for it, and the simulator's near-c rows carry the dilation factors.
demo_output:
Reference: Signature Walker at 1.4 m/s
100 km time (s): 71428.6
Earth-Moon time (days): 3177910.05
c = 299792458 m/s is the limit; this reference is far below c.

title: Signature Light Beam
body:
The Signature Light Beam is the Signature edition's light reference: 299,792,458 meters per second, exactly c, the absolute limit, stated in Signature framing with the same standard value.

Reference speed: 299792458.0 m/s. Time to cover 100 km at this speed: 333.564 microseconds; time to cover the Earth-Moon distance at this speed: 21.37 minutes; time to cover one astronomical unit: 5.78 days.

Its limit is the law itself: no massive object reaches c, and time dilation grows without bound near it. The Signature edition does not claim otherwise; it repeats the standard as the standard. Standard math: c = 299,792,458 m/s is the absolute limit; this reference is far below c, so time dilation is negligible for it, and the simulator's near-c rows carry the dilation factors.

title: Signature Earth Loop
body:
The Signature Earth Loop is the Signature edition's world-circumnavigation distance: 40,075 kilometers around a Signature Earth, a walk of years, a jet of about two days, and light in about one seventh of a second.

Distance: 40,075,000 km. Walking it takes 907.07 years; a highway car takes 42.33 years; a passenger jet takes 5.08 years; light takes 2.23 minutes, which is the one-way light-time delay for this distance.

Its limit is the same planet size as the public reference: the Signature edition mirrors the circumference with a new name, and its table answers are the standard answers. Standard math: the full simulator table rebuilds these times for every reference when the distance or the reference changes, and near-c rows show time dilation per special relativity, gamma = 1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2).

Distance: Signature Earth Loop (40,075,000 km)
Walking time (days): 331307.87
Light time (s): 133.68
Near-c dilation at 0.9c (gamma): 2.2942

body:
The Signature Star Step is one light-year: about 9.461 trillion kilometers, the distance light travels in one year, a distance that makes every slower reference absurd and every faster hope a matter of generations, not trips.

title: Signature Galaxy Hop
body:
The Signature Galaxy Hop is a hundred thousand light-years, roughly the diameter of the Milky Way: light takes a hundred thousand years to cross it, and every slower reference's answer runs to billions of years, which is the point of including it.

Its limit is the galaxy's size against c: no traveler crosses it in a lifetime, and the Signature edition includes the row so the table's absurd answers are read as scale lessons, not travel plans. title: Signature Near-Light Run
body:
The Signature Near-Light Run is a tenth of a light-year: about 946 billion kilometers, a distance chosen because at ninety percent of light speed the traveler's clock runs at less than half the stay-at-home rate, so time dilation becomes a readable number in the table.

Distance: 946,100,000,000,000 km. Walking it takes 21414357057.75 years; a highway car takes 999336662.70 years; a passenger jet takes 119920399.52 years; light takes 100.00 years, which is the one-way light-time delay for this distance.

Its limit is dilation itself: at 0.9c the factor is about 2.29, so the traveler ages less than half as much as those left behind. The Signature edition states the factor and the formula, and it never claims the run is buildable. Standard math: the full simulator table rebuilds these times for every reference when the distance or the reference changes, and near-c rows show time dilation per special relativity, gamma = 1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2).
